# Gaussian and Primitive-Based Representations


## Overview
This family builds on [Model Architecture Modifications](11313-model-architecture-modifications.md) by replacing the global implicit coordinate-to-radiance mapping of standard NeRF with explicit, learnable 3D primitives (Gaussians, quadrics, or neural points) to improve rendering efficiency and geometric fidelity [S1]. Unlike grid-based or pure MLP approaches, these methods represent the scene as a discrete set of elements, enabling differentiable rasterization or local neighborhood aggregation [S1]. This approach is distinct from [Signed Distance Function (SDF) Representations](12495-signed-distance-function-sdf-representations.md) by avoiding signed distance field constraints, and from [Voxel and Sparse Grid Representations](13738-voxel-and-sparse-grid-representations.md) by using continuous or parametric primitives rather than discrete volumetric cells [S1].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the following core mechanism:
1. **Explicit Representation:** The scene is defined by a set of $N$ learnable primitives $\mathcal{P} = \{p_i\}_{i=1}^N$ [S1]. Each primitive $p_i$ carries geometric parameters (e.g., position, covariance, quadric coefficients) and appearance parameters (e.g., color, opacity, feature vectors) [S1].
2. **Differentiability:** The rendering process is differentiable with respect to the primitive parameters [S1]. This allows gradients from the photometric loss to flow back to the primitive attributes, enabling end-to-end optimization via gradient descent [S1].
3. **Local or Explicit Evaluation:** Unlike global NeRFs that query a single MLP for any coordinate, these methods evaluate appearance based on local context (neighborhood aggregation) or explicit projection (rasterization) [S1].
4. **Alpha Compositing:** The final pixel color is computed via volume rendering equation:
$$ C = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} c_i \alpha_i \prod_{j < i} (1 - \alpha_j) $$
where $c_i$ is the color, $\alpha_i$ is the opacity, and the product term is the transmittance [S1]. The set $\mathcal{N}$ contains primitives intersecting the ray or projected to the pixel, sorted by depth [S1].

## Subtopics

### [Differentiable Primitive Assembly](13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md)
Models geometry as an assembly of learnable quadric primitives using differentiable Boolean operations (intersection/union). Chosen for structured abstraction of complex topologies like holes and thin structures.

### [Viewing Direction Gaussian Splatting](14273-viewing-direction-gaussian-splatting.md)
Combines 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization with a neural network that modulates Gaussian opacity based on viewing direction. Chosen to resolve view-dependent artifacts (e.g., glass reflections) while maintaining real-time rendering speeds.

### [Point-NeRF Representation](15538-point-nerf-representation.md)
Uses a discrete neural point cloud where density and radiance are regressed from local neighborhood features via inverse distance weighting. Chosen to avoid inefficient ray sampling in empty space and spectral bias of global MLPs.

### [Frequency-Modulated Point Cloud Rendering](15903-frequency-modulated-point-cloud-rendering.md)
Uses an Adaptive Frequency Net (AFNet) to modulate implicit radiance signals with local texture frequency encoding. Chosen for high-frequency detail reconstruction in point-based rendering, overcoming spectral bias.

### GARF
A method using Gaussian activations as an alternative to positional encoding in NeRF, combined with bundle adjustment for pose estimation from unknown camera poses [S1]. Uses Gaussian activations as an effective alternative to positional encoding, in conjunction with bundle adjustment for pose estimation [S1]. Successfully recovers scene representations from unknown camera poses in challenging scenes with low-textured regions [S1].

## Background
Originating from the need to address computational bottlenecks in ray-marching dense MLPs, early work like [Point-NeRF](15538-point-nerf-representation.md) demonstrated that point clouds could approximate scene geometry more efficiently than grids [S1]. Subsequent developments, such as [Differentiable Primitive Assembly](13657-differentiable-primitive-assembly.md) and quadric assemblies, leveraged differentiable rasterization to achieve real-time performance [S1]. In parallel, methods like GARF (April 2022) integrated Gaussian activations with bundle adjustment for pose estimation, successfully recovering scene representations from unknown camera poses in challenging low-textured regions [S1]. These methods are widely used in real-time rendering, SLAM, and scenes requiring high-frequency detail or complex topology [S1].
